description: Synthetic Claim-card case set v1 for the checker experiment (issue #3). Fifty cards across three fictional UK advice households, each pairing a Claim with Evidence Spans from fictional Source Artifacts and a human-checkable expected verdict.

provenance.statement: All households, people, employers, providers and figures are fictional and were written for this repository. Provider names are fictional except generic references to public schemes (the NHS Pension Scheme and the UK State Pension). No real client data, transcripts or firm material.

usage: The fields category, expected_verdict and rationale are ground truth for evaluation. A checker must only be shown claim and evidence_spans.

source_artifacts.title: Annual review meeting, Sharma-Patel, 17 April 2026
lines: Adviser (Sarah Hall): Good afternoon, both. This is our annual review, recorded for your file. Let's start with work and income.
Priya Sharma: I'm still at the hospital pharmacy. My basic salary went up to £68,500 with the April pay round, and I do the odd on-call weekend on top.
Dev Patel: Mine's £47,900 now that the leadership allowance is included.
Adviser (Sarah Hall): Thank you. Priya, your Aldgate plan was valued at £207,432 as at 5 April.
Priya Sharma: That's better than I expected. It was about £185,000 when we last did a full review, two years ago.
Adviser (Sarah Hall): And you're contributing 8% of basic salary, with the trust adding 5%.
Dev Patel: My Pennine statement came last week. I still find the teachers' scheme statements hard to read.
Adviser (Sarah Hall): The headline figures are the estimated annual pension of £19,150 at 65, and the lump sum of £57,450.
Priya Sharma: What happens if I add more to Aldgate? I could probably find £500 a month.
Adviser (Sarah Hall): At mid growth assumptions, adding £500 a month from now could take the plan to around £350,000 by your 60th birthday.
Adviser (Sarah Hall): It's a projection, not a promise — the actual figure will move with markets.
Priya Sharma: Understood. And if I stopped at 55 instead?
Adviser (Sarah Hall): If you retired at 55, the fund might support around £9,750 a year of drawdown income to age 75. Again, illustrative only.
Dev Patel: The Bramwell ISA is Priya's — I've never had one. What's in it now?
Priya Sharma: Around £42,000, I think. I really must check the statement.
Adviser (Sarah Hall): The mortgage next. Any changes?
Dev Patel: The Calderdale mortgage is down to about £186,000 on the last statement I looked at.
Adviser (Sarah Hall): We'll confirm against the annual statement — rounded recollections are how drafts drift.
Priya Sharma: Anything else before we close?
Adviser (Sarah Hall): That covers the annual review. We'll send the draft fact-find for your corrections.

source_artifacts.title: Retirement planning meeting, Okafor, 24 April 2026
lines: Adviser (Sarah Hall): Good morning. Today we're mapping the run-up to retirement, recorded for your file. Salaries first?
Chidi Okafor: Still £78,600, though the car allowance sits on top of that.
Ngozi Okafor: I'm on £54,300 now the ward manager uplift has gone through.
Adviser (Sarah Hall): Thank you. Chidi, your Meridian plan was valued at £366,400 as at 31 March.
Chidi Okafor: I'd have said it was sitting around £380,000, but I'll take the statement's word.
Adviser (Sarah Hall): It was about £340,000 at the spring 2024 review, so it's been a strong two years.
Chidi Okafor: The Meridian pot's come back well since the spring wobble, whatever the exact figure.
Ngozi Okafor: My NHS statement shows the annual pension at sixty is £21,850, with a lump sum of £65,550.
Adviser (Sarah Hall): And your State Pension forecasts. Chidi, yours is £214.85 a week from age 67.
Ngozi Okafor: What about the annuity option for my Meridian pot — sorry, Chidi's Meridian pot?
Adviser (Sarah Hall): The quote we have for the Meridian fund is £11,850 a year, level payments, single life, with a five-year guarantee.
Chidi Okafor: And if I took the tax-free cash first?
Adviser (Sarah Hall): If you took 25% tax-free cash from Meridian now, that would be around £91,600, and the rest would buy less income.
Adviser (Sarah Hall): These figures are illustrative — quotes move with the market.
Ngozi Okafor: My state pension forecast is the one I never remember.
Adviser (Sarah Hall): We'll attach both forecasts to the file rather than rely on memory today.
Chidi Okafor: Contributions — I put in £7,150 and the firm puts in £5,600, so £12,750 altogether in the year.
Adviser (Sarah Hall): That matches the statement. Anything else before we summarise?
Ngozi Okafor: Nothing from me.
Adviser (Sarah Hall): We'll send the draft fact-find for corrections.

source_artifacts.title: Later-life planning review, Whitfield, 12 May 2026
lines: Adviser (Sarah Hall): Good afternoon, Margaret. This is your later-life planning review, recorded for your file. How are things?
Margaret Whitfield: Steady, thank you. The Dunston pot's about £225,000 still, I believe.
Adviser (Sarah Hall): We'll check that against the statement in a moment.
Margaret Whitfield: It was £260,000 when I started taking the income in 2021, before the markets wobbled.
Adviser (Sarah Hall): The Dunston fund has recovered nicely since the autumn dip.
Adviser (Sarah Hall): Your own pension from teaching is £14,050 a year, and the survivor's pension from Alan's Sefton scheme is £4,620 a year.
Margaret Whitfield: Alan's scheme pays me about £4,400 a year I think — it's never the figure I remember.
Adviser (Sarah Hall): Your State Pension is £230.25 a week now after the April uprating.
Margaret Whitfield: And I take £950 a month from the Dunston pot, into the bank on the fifteenth.
Adviser (Sarah Hall): We should confirm how much of that is taxable at your marginal rate.
Adviser (Sarah Hall): On care fees, it's worth planning ahead. If care fees of £1,200 a week were needed, the combined pot would last about nine and a half years.
Adviser (Sarah Hall): That's an illustration for planning, not a forecast of what care will cost.
Margaret Whitfield: When Alan died we had about £92,000 in savings; it's less now, what with the new boiler and the trip to see my sister in Toronto.
Adviser (Sarah Hall): The Eastgate statement will show where the savings stand now.
Adviser (Sarah Hall): Anything else you'd like to look at?
Margaret Whitfield: Only that I don't want to be a burden on Deborah — she's got enough on her plate.
Adviser (Sarah Hall): Understood, we'll keep the withdrawal plan under review with that in mind.
Margaret Whitfield: That's reassuring.
Adviser (Sarah Hall): We'll send the draft fact-find for your corrections.
[Meeting ends]
